Published in final edited form as: Biol Psychiatry Cogn Neurosci Neuroimaging. 2019 Jan 25;4(7):610–618. doi: 10.1016/j.bpsc.2019.01.005 Abstract Background: In the search for novel treatments for depression, ketamine has emerged as a unique agent with rapid antidepressant effects. Experimental tasks involving emotional processing can be used during functional MRI (fMRI) scanning to investigate ketamine’s effects on brain function in major depressive disorder (MDD). This study examined ketamine’s effects on fMRI activity during an emotional processing task. Methods: Thirty-three individuals with treatment-resistant MDD and 24 healthy controls (HCs) took part in this double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover study. Participants received ketamine and placebo infusions two weeks apart, and fMRI scans were conducted at baseline and two days after each infusion. Blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal was measured during an emotional processing task, and a linear mixed-effects model was used to analyze differences in activation between group, drug, and task-specific factors. Results: A group-by-drug interaction was observed in several brain regions, including a right frontal cluster extending into the anterior cingulate cortex and insula. MDD participants had greater activity than HCs after placebo infusion but showed lower activity after ketamine infusion, which was similar to the activity in HCs after placebo. A group-by-drug-by-task condition interaction was also found, which showed further differences that varied between implicit and explicit emotional conditions. Conclusions: The main results indicate that ketamine had differential effects on brain activity in MDD versus HC participants. The pattern of activation in MDD participants post-ketamine resembled the activation in HCs post-placebo, suggesting a normalization of function during emotional processing. The findings contribute to a better understanding of ketamine’s actions in the brain. Nevertheless, most treatments for major depressive disorder (MDD) only benefit a fraction of all individuals with the disorder, and current antidepressants often take weeks to have an effect. Recent research has shown that ketamine, a glutamatergic modulator, has rapid antidepressant effects in MDD and in treatment-resistant depression (2-5). Broadly, neuroimaging research has been used to study differences between individuals with MDD and healthy controls (HCs), particularly in relation to emotional processing. Previous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) research found increased activation in prefrontal and limbic regions in participants with MDD during emotion regulation, along with differences in areas of the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), as shown by a review of various emotion-related tasks (6). Specifically, studies found increased activity in ventro-rostral ACC and decreased activity in dorsal ACC during the viewing of emotional stimuli, including pictures, faces, and words (7). With regard to valence of emotion, studies have shown increased response to negative stimuli in emotional processing regions in MDD participants, and decreased response to positive stimuli, found in a meta-analysis of multiple types of emotion processing tasks (8) and in a review of emotional face processing tasks (9). This may represent a bias towards negative stimuli and has even been observed with implicit viewing of emotional faces in a backward masking task (10). It should be noted, however, that varied findings in the literature suggest that both increases and decreases in activation are associated with valence of emotional stimuli. Behaviorally, emotional processing biases have often been found in MDD, with greater attention towards negative and away from positive emotional stimuli (11, 12). fMRI has also been used in depressive disorders-related research to investigate the effects of pharmacologic treatment on blood-oxygen-level dependent (BOLD) signal in the brain. In general, traditional antidepressants have been found to normalize brain function in areas of under- or over-activation in participants with MDD (as compared to HCs) (13, 14). An attenuated response to negative stimuli and an increased response to positive stimuli has also been found in conjunction with implicit processing of emotion after antidepressant treatment in the ACC (17). In this context, neuroimaging studies—and fMRI in particular—are a valuable way to explore how ketamine affects brain function in MDD. To date, only a few studies have investigated ketamine’s effects on brain activity during emotional processing. In one study, ketamine increased activation in the right caudate of participants with MDD while they viewed positive faces (14), though it should be noted that this study lacked a placebo control. Introduction Currently available FDA-approved pharmacological treatments for major depressive disorder (MDD) take several weeks to achieve their full antidepressant effects, thus significantly impacting patient function and well-being and underscoring the urgent need for faster-acting medications to treat this disorder. The glutamatergic modulator ketamine has rapid antidepressant effects (Berman et al., 2000), even in treatment-resistant MDD (Zarate Jr. et al., 2006). However, much remains unknown about ketamine's precise mechanism of action in the brain, including its effects on neurobiology and specific depressive symptomatology. In this regard, it would be valuable to examine the effects of ketamine on cognitive and affective processing domains, with particular interest in those previously found to differ in MDD, such as emotion processing. Specifically, numerous behavioral studies have suggested that, compared to healthy controls (HCs), individuals with MDD demonstrate a cognitive bias towards negative emotional information (Dalgleish and Watts, 1990; Mathews and Macleod, 1994). For instance, studies have reported biases for stimuli including depression- and anxiety-related words (Mogg et al., 1995), socially threatening words (Mathews et al., 1996), and sad faces (Gotlib et al., 2004; Joormann and Gotlib, 2007). However, some studies have also noted the absence of a behavioral bias in depression, such as with angry, sad, happy (Mogg et al., 2000), or fearful (Amico et al., 2012) facial expressions. Dot probe attentional bias tasks have been used with emotion-related word and face stimuli to assess cognitive biases in depressed participants (Peckham et al., 2010). Generally in a dot probe task, two different stimuli are presented for a short time, followed by a dot in the same location as one of the prior stimuli. The participant responds to indicate the location of the dot, and reaction time is measured to analyze attentional bias towards a specific type of stimulus. Thus, the task can span both attentional and emotional processing domains. Notably, the administration of dot probe tasks during functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can identify brain regions associated with attentional bias towards or away from certain emotional stimuli. In general, neuroimaging findings may also be more stable (based on test-retest reliability) and sensitive than behavioral measures of attentional bias using this type of task (White et al., 2016). For example, fMRI results associated with a dot probe task showed activation differences between MDD participants and HCs associated with fearful stimuli in the absence of behavioral differences that would be consistent with an attentional bias; specifically, MDD participants had less activation in the left middle cingulum and left insula (Amico et al., 2012). Other fMRI research using dot probe tasks showed increased activation in temporo-parietal and occipito-parietal regions in response to fearful versus happy faces in HCs (Pourtois et al., 2006). In addition, decreased anterior cingulate cortex activation was found during incongruent trials across healthy and anxious youth participants (Price et al., 2014). In addition to probing baseline differences in emotional processing, dot probe tasks can also be used to investigate neuroimaging changes associated with the influence of treatment. For instance, multiple dot probe studies have demonstrated the effects of anxiolytic treatments on attentional biases and related changes in the brain (Britton et al., 2015; Ironside et al., 2016); to date, however, research into treatment approaches for depression using dot probe tasks has been limited. Due to its rapid onset and short duration of action, ketamine is uniquely suited to studying antidepressant response using cognitive tasks and fMRI. Indeed, recent research has examined ketamine's effects on cognitive and emotional processing using other cognitive tasks, though no studies have yet examined dot probe tasks specifically. Ketamine would also be expected to affect individuals with treatment-resistant MDD, given its demonstrated effects as a glutamatergic modulator and the potential dysfunctions of the glutamate system associated with depression (Niciu et al., 2014; Zarate Jr. et al., 2010). In an emotion perception task, participants with treatment-resistant MDD showed increased activation in response to positive emotion in the right caudate after ketamine treatment (Murrough et al., 2015), but this study included no placebo condition for comparison. In a working memory task with emotional stimuli in HCs, ketamine decreased activity in the left and right insula and right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) specifically during negative emotion conditions (Scheidegger et al., 2016a). In HCs who received a single ketamine infusion, reduced activation was observed in an amygdalo-hippocampal area during emotional processing (Scheidegger et al., 2016b), as was greater deactivation in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) in response to negative stimuli (Lehmann et al., 2016). While these studies investigated ketamine's effects using fMRI, only limited conclusions can be drawn, given that they did not involve simultaneous longitudinal assessments of both MDD and HC participants, and most lacked a placebo control condition. However, ketamine’s effects on emotional processing biases remain largely unknown, and understanding these processes may help elucidate ketamine’s mechanism of action. Methods: Magnetoencephalography (MEG) was used to investigate ketamine’s effects on early visual responses to affective stimuli in individuals with MDD (n=31) and healthy volunteers (HVs; n=24). Abstract Background Prior studies suggest that the amygdala shapes complex behavioral responses to socially ambiguous cues. We explored human amygdala function during explicit behavioral decision making about discrete emotional facial expressions that can represent socially unambiguous and ambiguous cues. Methods During functional magnetic resonance imaging, 43 healthy adults were required to make complex social decisions (i.e., approach or avoid) about either relatively unambiguous (i.e., angry, fearful, happy) or ambiguous (i.e., neutral) facial expressions. Reaction times to neutral expressions were longer than those to angry, fearful, and happy expressions during social judgment only. Imaging data on stimuli judged to be avoided revealed a significant task by emotion interaction in the amygdala. Here, only neutral facial expressions elicited greater activity during social judgment than during sex discrimination. Furthermore, during social judgment only, neutral faces judged to be avoided were associated with greater amygdala activity relative to neutral faces that were judged as approachable. Moreover, functional coupling between the amygdala and both dorsolateral prefrontal (social judgment > sex discrimination) and cingulate (sex discrimination > social judgment) cortices was differentially modulated by task during processing of neutral faces. Conclusions Our results suggest that increased amygdala reactivity and differential functional coupling with prefrontal circuitries may shape complex decisions and behavioral responses to socially ambiguous cues. Paramount to such efforts is the ability to resolve the nature of socially ambiguous information or uncertain contexts, that is, social inputs that do not provide enough information about the social action to take, which may be interpreted as threatening. Recent studies have demonstrated that in addition to its critical contribution to fear-related behaviors (1), the amygdala, which is functionally connected with prefrontal and cingulate regions (2–4) and associated with regulation of emotional responses (5), contributes to more complex social behaviors and is sensitive to socially ambiguous stimuli (6). For example, lesions of the amygdala are associated with increased trustworthiness ratings of unfamiliar neutral faces (7), whereas the magnitude of amygdala activation observed with functional neuroimaging is associated with decreased trustworthiness ratings (8). Moreover, the amygdala exhibits a strong response to novel, emotionally neutral facial expressions that diminishes with familiarity (9,10), a pattern consistent with the initially ambiguous nature of such stimuli (i.e., neither emotionally positive nor negative and potentially threatening). In addition, the amygdala responds to increasing relative ambiguity of explicitly emotional facial expressions as a function of experimental manipulation (11). These findings suggest that the amygdala, through its capacity to increase behavioral and physiological arousal, as well as through processing of both cue- and context-related information, may be recruited for explicit responses to socially ambiguous cues (6,12,13). In this study, we explored the contribution of the amygdala to explicit behavioral decisions about socially ambiguous stimuli. Forty-three healthy adults completed an event-related blood oxygen level–dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance (fMRI) study during which they were required to make complex, explicit social decisions (i.e., approach or avoid) about facial stimuli with relatively unambiguous (i.e., angry, fearful, or happy) or ambiguous (i.e., neutral) emotional expressions. We hypothesized that both decision-making processes on unambiguous stimuli with negative valence (i.e., angry and fearful facial expressions) would be associated with amygdala response because they are perceived as aversive regardless of the cognitive context within which responses are given. By contrast, when the stimuli are emotionally ambiguous, the context within which to give behavioral responses may affect activity of the amygdala. Neurobiological mechanism branch

Ketamine’s effects are best understood as involving a combination of glutamatergic disruption, NMDA receptor antagonism, and downstream reorganization of cortical and subcortical networks. The evidence points to ketamine’s primary mechanism as blocking NMDA receptors, which are glutamate-gated ion channels, and thereby altering excitatory neurotransmission. This action is central to ketamine’s rapid antidepressant effects and broader neuroplastic effects. In the evidence provided, ketamine is described as blocking inhibitory neurotransmitters and as a glutamatergic modulator that relieves depression by blocking NMDA, a glutamate receptor [N1-R5], while another source notes that ketamine relieves depression by blocking NMDA, a glutamate receptor, with glutamate being an excitatory neurotransmitter [N4-R5]. This suggests that ketamine’s main neurochemical impact is not merely inhibitory but rather a disruption of glutamatergic signaling through NMDA antagonism.

The downstream effects are not confined to one receptor or one region. The evidence indicates that ketamine promotes synaptogenesis in brain regions such as the medial frontal cortex and hippocampus, countering dendritic atrophy [N1-R1], and it is linked to neuroplastic changes that help the brain form healthier emotional and cognitive pathways [N1-R2]. This implies that ketamine affects broader neural architecture rather than a single pathway. The provided evidence also notes that ketamine acutely acts on several brain systems involved in negative emotional processing by decreasing reactivity and that it modulates cognition-emotion interaction by inducing lateralized and valence-specific effects [N4-R3][N4-R2]. These statements support the idea that ketamine’s effects are not static but dynamically reshape brain function, particularly in negative-emotion circuits.

Regarding brain regions and networks, the evidence implicates several key areas. The medial frontal cortex and hippocampus are directly mentioned as regions where ketamine promotes synaptogenesis [N1-R1]. More broadly, ketamine studies in emotional processing have implicated the prefrontal cortex, limbic regions, amygdala, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex, with some reports noting differential effects on these structures depending on whether participants are depressed or healthy [N2-F1][N2-F2]. For example, one fMRI study found that ketamine decreased amygdala, hippocampus, insula, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex activity in healthy controls during emotional processing [N2-F2]. Another study noted that ketamine suppressed parahippocampal and medial prefrontal activity irrespective of emotion, while ketamine also showed emotion-specific effects [N1-R4]. The evidence therefore supports a distributed network model, with the prefrontal cortex, limbic system, and subcortical regions such as the amygdala and hippocampus all implicated.

On the timeline of effects, the evidence suggests both acute and possibly longer-term changes. The strongest direct evidence for acute effects comes from the statement that ketamine “acutely acts on several brain systems involved in negative emotional processing” [N4-R3]. Another source notes that ketamine’s antidepressant effects are rapid and that repeated administration can produce a sustained response [N4-R5]. The evidence also mentions that one pilot study tested the potential of a single infusion of ketamine, followed by brief exposure therapy, to enhance post-retrieval extinction of PTSD [N1-R3]. This suggests that ketamine can have acute effects, and its effects may be extended through repeated exposure, though the provided evidence does not establish a long-term sustained effect with certainty. The distinction matters because acute effects are more directly tied to immediate glutamatergic disruption and downstream synaptic changes, whereas subacute or repeated exposure may involve adaptation, tolerance, or additional neuroplastic remodeling, which is not fully resolved in the provided evidence [N1-R3][N4-R3].

In short, the neurobiological mechanism branch is best summarized as: ketamine blocks NMDA glutamate receptors, disrupts glutamatergic transmission, and thereby alters excitatory signaling; this initiates acute changes in brain regions such as the medial frontal cortex, hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, limbic structures, amygdala, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex; and these effects are likely acute, with possible longer-term or repeated-exposure effects that the provided evidence suggests but does not fully detail [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N4-R2][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Imaging/behavioral evidence branch

The evidence shows that ketamine alters brain activation during emotional processing, but the specific facial expressions showing altered activation vary by study and by participant group. The strongest direct fMRI evidence comes from a double-blind placebo-controlled study in which ketamine had differential effects on brain activity in major depressive disorder (MDD) versus healthy control (HC) participants [N2-F1]. In this study, a group-by-drug interaction was observed in several brain regions, including a right frontal cluster extending into the anterior cingulate cortex and insula. MDD participants had greater activity than HCs after placebo infusion, but showed lower activity after ketamine infusion, which was similar to HC activity after placebo [N2-F1]. This suggests that ketamine changes brain activation during emotional processing, but the pattern differs between MDD and HC participants.

The same study also found a group-by-drug-by-task condition interaction, showing further differences that varied between implicit and explicit emotional conditions [N2-F1]. This indicates that activation changes are not uniform across all emotional conditions and depend on the nature of the task. The evidence further notes that ketamine decreased activity in the amygdala, hippocampus, insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and pregenual ACC in HC participants during emotional processing [N2-F1]. In contrast, in MDD participants, ketamine increased activity in the right caudate during viewing of positive faces, though this study lacked a placebo control [N2-F1]. These findings imply that ketamine’s effects are expression- and group-dependent, rather than expression-independent.

The electrophysiological evidence in MDD also shows altered responses to emotional faces, but with different temporal signatures. A magnetoencephalography (MEG) study found that ketamine altered emotional stimulus processing in MDD, with M100 amplitudes becoming more similar between MDD and healthy volunteers after ketamine and with fusiform M170 amplitudes associated with antidepressant response in MDD participants [N3-F3]. The study also reported that baseline behavioral analyses showed MDD participants had higher accuracy for sad-angry than happy-neutral faces, while healthy volunteers responded faster to happy-neutral than sad-angry faces [N3-F3]. This behavioral evidence suggests that ketamine’s effects extend beyond brain activation to emotion recognition and processing speed, but the provided evidence is more indirect than the fMRI findings.

On the contrasts and statistical thresholds used in the studies, the fMRI study explicitly used a linear mixed-effects model to analyze differences in activation between group, drug, and task-specific factors [N2-F1]. It also noted that the results indicated differential findings in MDD versus HC participants [N2-F1]. The MEG study used linear fixed effects models to examine interactions between diagnosis, stimulus valence, and drug session for behavioral and MEG data [N3-F3]. While the provided excerpts do not give explicit statistical thresholds, the methodological emphasis on mixed-effects and fixed-effects modeling supports the conclusion that the studies used rigorous statistical frameworks to compare groups and conditions [N2-F1][N3-F3].

Overall, the imaging and behavioral evidence suggests that ketamine alters brain activation during emotional processing, but the specific facial expressions and activation patterns are not consistent across studies. The evidence is strongest for MDD versus HC differences and for emotion-specific effects in healthy controls, while the effects vary across expression types and participant groups [N2-F1][N3-F3]. The use of mixed-effects and fixed-effects models indicates that the studies attempted to control for between- and within-subject variability, but the evidence still leaves room for heterogeneity across samples and conditions [N2-F1][N3-F3].

Study design and interpretation branch

Study designs differ substantially by modality, sample size, and control conditions. The evidence includes fMRI, MEG, and behavioral studies, each with different strengths and weaknesses. The fMRI study described was a double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover design with 33 MDD participants and 24 healthy controls, and it included baseline and post-infusion fMRI scans [N2-F1]. The MEG study was also a double-blind, placebo-controlled, crossover clinical trial with 31 MDD participants and 24 healthy volunteers, with assessments at baseline and after subanesthetic-dose ketamine and placebo-saline infusions [N3-F3]. These designs are strong because they include control conditions and repeated measures, reducing confounding from time-related effects and allowing within-subject comparisons [N2-F1][N3-F3].

Sample size is another important design factor. The fMRI study had 33 MDD and 24 HC participants, while the MEG study had 31 MDD and 24 HV participants [N2-F1][N3-F3]. These are relatively modest sample sizes, which can reduce statistical power and limit generalizability. The MEG study explicitly notes that the modest sample size and the need to collapse across responses to happy and neutral faces to increase statistical power limit the generalizability of the findings [N3-F3]. This is an important limitation because small samples can lead to inflated effect sizes or false positives, and collapsing data can obscure expression-specific patterns [N3-F3].

Control conditions also differ across the studies. The fMRI study used placebo control and baseline comparisons, and the MEG study likewise used placebo-saline infusions and baseline assessments [N2-F1][N3-F3]. However, not all studies had strong control conditions. For example, one earlier fMRI study in MDD participants lacked a placebo control [N2-F1]. Another study in healthy controls reported decreased activation in the amygdala, hippocampus, insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and pregenual ACC during emotional processing, but the excerpt does not explicitly say whether a placebo control was included [N2-F1]. The lack of placebo control limits the ability to distinguish ketamine’s true effects from placebo or acute-task effects.

Limitations include small sample size, medication use, and acute versus chronic exposure. The provided evidence emphasizes that the MEG study had a modest sample size and that collapsing responses to happy and neutral faces was needed to increase power [N3-F3]. The fMRI study also notes that most previous studies lacked a placebo control, which limits conclusions [N2-F1]. In addition, the evidence suggests that ketamine effects are acute in nature, as one study describes ketamine as acting acutely on negative-emotion systems [N4-R3]. Another source notes that repeated ketamine exposure can lead to addiction with psychological dependence and cognitive issues such as memory lapses and executive function impairments [N6-R3]. This matters because acute effects may differ from chronic or repeated exposure, and the provided evidence suggests that repeated use may introduce additional confounding factors such as tolerance, dependence, or cognitive side effects [N6-R3].

Distinguishing true effects from confounding factors requires careful interpretation. The evidence shows that ketamine effects can be group-specific: in MDD participants, ketamine reduced activity in some regions and increased activity in the right caudate during positive-face viewing; in healthy controls, ketamine decreased activity in amygdala, hippocampus, insula, and pregenual ACC [N2-F1]. This supports the idea that ketamine’s effects are not uniform and may reflect normalization in MDD rather than a general effect across all groups [N2-F1]. The MEG study also found that M100 amplitudes became more similar between MDD and healthy volunteers after ketamine, and that fusiform M170 amplitudes were associated with antidepressant response [N3-F3]. This suggests that some effects may be task- or response-specific, and that true ketamine effects must be separated from task-related, behavioral, or placebo-related changes [N3-F3]. Overall, the best interpretation is that the studies support acute ketamine effects, but the evidence is heterogeneous and subject to small-sample, control, and group-specific limitations [N2-F1][N3-F3][N6-R3].

The strongest fMRI evidence comes from a study showing that ketamine had differential effects on brain activity in MDD versus healthy control participants [N2-F1]. In that study, a group-by-drug interaction was observed in several brain regions, including a right frontal cluster extending into the anterior cingulate cortex and insula. MDD participants showed greater activity than HCs after placebo infusion, but lower activity after ketamine infusion, which was similar to HC activity after placebo [N2-F1]. This suggests that ketamine’s effects are not uniform across all facial expressions or all groups.

The same study also found a group-by-drug-by-task condition interaction, showing further differences that varied between implicit and explicit emotional conditions [N2-F1]. This is important because it indicates that activation changes are not merely valence-dependent but also task-dependent. In healthy controls, ketamine decreased activity in the amygdala, hippocampus, insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and pregenual ACC during emotional processing [N2-F1]. In MDD participants, ketamine increased activity in the right caudate during viewing of positive faces, though this study lacked a placebo control [N2-F1]. These findings suggest that ketamine may suppress activation in some negative- or emotionally loaded circuits while increasing activation in specific positive-face circuits in MDD, but the evidence is mixed and group-specific [N2-F1].

The electrophysiological evidence also points to valence-specific changes. In MDD participants, ketamine altered emotional stimulus processing, with M100 amplitudes becoming more similar between MDD and healthy volunteers after ketamine and with fusiform M170 amplitudes associated with antidepressant response in MDD participants [N3-F3]. The behavioral evidence further shows that baseline MDD participants had higher accuracy for sad-angry than happy-neutral faces, while healthy volunteers responded faster to happy-neutral than sad-angry faces [N3-F3]. This suggests that ketamine may reduce the valence-related bias in MDD, at least in some measures, but the evidence is not expression-specific enough to identify a single “neutral,” “positive,” or “negative” pattern.
